title: Australia news live: transport regulator investigating two more incidents at Sydney airport, taking tally to six in a month
text:
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has confirmed it will investigate two new incidents on Sydney airport’s taxiways this month.
The new incidents being investigated occurred on 16 August, a taxiing conflict involving a Virgin and Qantas aircraft, and on 25 August, an air traffic control miscommunication with the pilots of a Jetstar aircraft.
The investigations add to a list of reported near collisions and other safety incidents since the beginning of the month, when major delays and cancellations affected both domestic and international flights.
Here is a rundown of the reported incidents:
27 July: a Qantas flight was cleared to cross a runway in front of another of the airline’s planes that had just landed.
9 August: a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided hitting a Qatar Airways plane that was pulled across the runway in front of it.
9 August: a Virgin plane was forced to abort take-off when a Qantas plane began to cross the runway in front of it
16 August: a taxiing conflict involving a Boeing aircraft and a Virgin Australia aircraft.
18 August: another taxiing conflict involving a Boeing aircraft and a Qantas aircraft.
25 August: a taxiing conflict involving a Jetstar aircraft that failed to give way to other traffic.
That’s a wrap on our live coverage.
Before we go, let’s take a look at the top headlines:
The prime minister, premiers and chief ministers have met today for a national cabinet meeting to discuss key issues including datacentre site, gender violence and gun reforms.
A man has been charged after allegedly punching a young boy and stabbing his mother with a pair of scissors in a random attack outside a police station in Melbourne’s CBD.
Tributes for the late Dolly Parton flowed this morning, including from the prime minister who said the singer had “made our world a better place in so many ways”.
Angela Jackson, the commissioner of the Productivity Commission, backed the body’s interim report into the GST, which found the deal with Western Australia to be a costly mistake that should be reversed.
Woolworths’ net profit has boomed 18% to $1.14bn as customers face cost-of-living pressures, the company has reported.
The Victorian government secretly increased public transport fares to raise money to help pay for the Suburban Rail Loop and other Big Build projects.
Nine Entertainment has lifted its annual earnings as it continues to focus on its streaming and broadcast assets, including Stan, 9Now and digital publishing.
Inflation has dropped to 3.5% in the year to July, from 3.8%, as fuel prices rebounded in the month and building costs jumped.
NSW police are investigating after 400,000 juvenile oysters, worth an estimated $350,000, were stolen near Taree on the state’s mid north coast earlier this year.
Silence has hung over a picturesque police station as hundreds stood in respect to mark one year since two officers were gunned down by Dezi Freeman.
Edge Early Learning, a major childcare provider with centres in Queensland, South Australia and the ACT, has gone into voluntary administration.
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has confirmed it will investigate two new incidents on Sydney airport’s taxiways this month.
Thanks for sticking around, see you tomorrow!

Roger Cook brushes off criticism of ‘east coast clowns’ sledge
Roger Cook, the Western Australian premier, has not apologised for referring to Productivity Commission officials as “east coast clowns”, saying “I’m doing exactly what I’ll always do and putting WA first”.
The Productivity Commission’s review process is not over yet, so it is important we continue to present our economic arguments.
Cook has come under fire for his sledge, triggered by the PC’s interim report last week which described the Morrison government’s sweetheart GST deal with WA as a costly mistake that should be reversed.
Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, this afternoon backed his top independent economic advisory body, saying the WA Labor leader’s insult was inappropriate.
The independent MP Allegra Spender described Cook’s name-calling as “simply unacceptable”.
But Cook was defiant, in a statement saying that “to the Productivity Commission it may be academic but for Western Australians it’s our lives, and I’ll fight for every dollar”.
Cook said he was advised that a meeting between his treasurer, Rita Saffioti, and PC officials on Wednesday to discuss the inquiry was “positive, polite and robust”. He said:
One thing the Productivity Commission’s report didn’t do is acknowledge Western Australia’s massive contribution to the national economy. They also didn’t explain why this report is so different to their 2018 report.
Victorian legal advocates oppose potential new police powers to allow officers access to people’s financial records without warrant
The Federation of Community Legal Centres says it is “deeply concerned” about proposed police powers that would allow officers to access a person’s financial records without a judge-issued warrant.
The proposed powers, which would apply to all offences, are part of upper-house amendments to crime reforms that have passed Victoria’s lower house.
The chief executive, Louisa Gibbs, described the changes as “frightening” and raised serious privacy concerns.
The proposed powers will allow police to authorise themselves to obtain information without notifying the person who holds the bank account and without a warrant.
The process of independent judicial consideration before granting police a warrant is an important check that our community expects and deserves.
Removing this step presents an unacceptable risk to the rights of all Victorians, and this amendment should be immediately withdrawn.
‘It is hard to imagine a world without her’: Albanese pays tribute to Dolly Parton during national cabinet media address
Continuing on that Sydney press conference, the prime minister has taken a moment to pay tribute to the late Dolly Parton. He said:
Dolly Parton made our world a better place in so many ways. It is hard to imagine a world without her. A singer and songwriter of rare power and talent, she also shone brightly as an actor, an author and a philanthropist who made such a contribution to promoting education around the world, as well as funding hospitals and making an enormous difference.
She had such an extraordinarily large personality and was much loved here in Australia and around the world … there will be a lot of broken hearts in Australia today and may I just say that Dolly Parton, I’m sure will rest in peace.
She lived loudly and she lived a great life. She will be much missed.
State and territory leaders and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, have agreed to further tighten national gun laws in a meeting in Sydney.
Albanese said federal government intelligence would be shared with state and territory law enforcement agencies as part of the deal, and that only Australian citizens would be allowed to hold gun licences.
The push comes after the deaths in December’s antisemitic shooting at Bondi Beach and as the federal government’s national buyback plan falters due to low take-up by the states. Only NSW and the ACT have signed up so far.
Albanese said 3D printed gun technology would be banned, along with sharing of materials about their production.
The prime minister, premiers and chief ministers have just held a press conference in Sydney after today’s national cabinet meeting.
Anthony Albanese outlined the key items they discussed:
Working together to form new artificial intelligence laws that he says will be legislated next year. They will also ensure power prices are protected and datacentres are located in the right places;
Accelerating policies to end gender-based violence;
Signing a new firearms agreement, aimed at improving laws after the Bondi massacre;
An additional $125m will be committed as part of the fight against bird flu;
Fuel security will continue to be monitored as the conflict in the Middle East reaches its six-month mark this week
Albanese described the meeting as “an excellent meeting” and thanked the panel for their “constructive engagement”.
Family violence advocates call for government’s commitment to action after national cabinet
The No to Violence chief executive, Phillip Ripper, has called on the national cabinet to commit to tangible action that prevents violence, intervenes earlier and holds men who use violence accountable.
He said:
Consultation on the next National Action Plan has reinforced a clear message to governments: more of the same will not deliver the change Australia needs. While we must keep doing everything possible to keep women and children safe, we will never see the dial shift until we tackle the problem at the source.
Australia spends billions of dollars every year responding to the consequences of men’s use of family violence, while police and courts across the country remain under enormous pressure. Yet comparatively little is invested in prevention, early intervention, holding men accountable for their behaviour, and providing effective pathways away from violence.
With Nick Visser off, I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of the afternoon’s news!
Teenage girl spared prison in first ‘adult time’ sentence
The first child to be sentenced under Victoria’s “adult time for violent crime” laws has been spared jail for a brazen and violent aggravated carjacking.
The 16-year-old girl, who cannot be named, was instead sentenced to an 18-month youth justice supervision order for the 27 February incident.
The teenager admitted she threatened a taxi driver with a knife before stealing his car about two hours after the “adult time” legislation came into effect.
Under the changes, children aged 14 and older who commit home invasions or aggravated carjackings must face the county court, where penalties are tougher than a children’s court.
Victorian county court judge Scott Johns found the offending was “brazen and violent”.
But her upbringing and the absence of any criminal record meant she should be sentenced under the Children’s Act.
The judge said on Wednesday:
Specific deterrence and protection of the community would be best served by your rehabilitation in the community.
No doubt for many cases of aggravated carjacking, sentences imposed under the (adult) Sentencing Act will be necessary.
I’ve concluded your case is not one of them.
He noted it was her first time before the courts and she had a difficult upbringing, having been in and out of child protection and residential care since the age of two.
– AAP
Sarah Hanson-Young condemns Malcolm Roberts’s comments about gay rights
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young had a scathing take on One Nation MP Malcolm Roberts being “in two minds” about gay rights.
Roberts made the comments when he was questioned about the party’s director, James Ashby.
Hanson-Young said this afternoon it “should be absolutely obvious” that LGBTQ+ Australians are indeed equal:
No one should be in two minds about that … that every Australian is equal. And I question Malcolm Roberts. He says he’s in two minds about this. Well, I wonder whether he’s even got one.
Edge Early Learning, a major childcare provider with centres in Queensland, South Australia and the ACT, has gone into voluntary administration.
The company will continue to operate all centres on a “business-as-usual basis’ with no change to care arrangements or opening hours and staffing.
The company said on its website:
We understand that this may be a confusing and stressful development for families who rely upon Edge Early Learning to provide care for their children.
Hi there, I’ll now be with you for the next little while.
That’s all for me. Jordyn Beazley will take things from here. Take care.
Jess Wilson says secret levy to help fund Suburban Rail Loop is ‘the final nail in the coffin’ for Victorian government
The Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has described the revelation public transport users have been paying a secret levy to help fund the Suburban Rail Loop as “the final nail in the coffin for this government”.
An auditor general report into the first stage of the SRL – from Cheltenham to Box Hill – tabled in parliament this morning, revealed the government added a 1% levy on public transport fares on 1 January 2025 but did not inform Victorians.
The auditor general said 60% of the revenue earned will go to SRL East.
The premier, Ben Carroll, was public transport minister when the levy was approved in 2021.
Speaking outside parliament this afternoon, Wilson said:
When VAGO handed down this report today, I expected to see cost blowouts. I expected to see delays to this project, but never in my wildest dreams did I think that there would be secret taxes levied on Victorians.
She said Carroll has “lied to Victorians” – and questioned “How many more secret taxes are there?”
Wilson went on:
This is just the final nail in the coffin for this government. I think we’ve seen a government that will lie to Victorians time and time and time again but hiding this, and for the auditor general to expose it, for the premier to fail to be upfront with Victorians at any point in time when he signed off on this, when he went to the 2022 election, when he became the premier of this state, it just demonstrates Ben Carroll has no integrity.
